title: Nitrophyte lichen share on US forest plots in 2000-2010 followed dry, warm climate, calcium dust and low sulfur, not reduced nitrogen, and did not change in five years on 203 resurveyed plots
abstract: Question: in standardized USDA FIA epiphytic macrolichen surveys, does the nitrophyte share of the species list follow reduced nitrogen (NHx) deposition, as the ammonia explanation predicts, or sulfur, calcium (dust) deposition and climate? This is an independent test of a British result (sci:d25508042db9) that nitrophyte gains did not follow NHx. Data: 1,700 surveys on 1,497 plots in 21 contiguous states (2000-2010), TDep 3-year deposition grids (NHx, oxidised N, S, Ca) and 1981-2010 nClimGrid climate. Method: binomial models of genus-level nitrophyte and sensitive-lichen counts with cluster-robust errors, state fixed effects, West/East splits and leave-one-state-out prediction; a resurvey test on 203 interior-West plots surveyed twice, five years apart. Results: NHx had no clear term (+0.11 log-odds per SD, 95% CI -0.08 to +0.29; West -0.06), and adding NHx made out-of-state prediction worse. Dry climate (precipitation -0.83), warmth (+0.20), Ca deposition (+0.67) and low S deposition (S -1.57) explained the share, also inside states. A positive eastern NHx term (+0.67) cannot be separated from correlated exposures. Only Xanthomendoza, Xanthoria and Candelaria followed NHx (+0.34). On resurveyed plots the nitrophyte share did not change (+0.004, -0.09 to +0.10) although the spatial deposition terms predicted +0.48; a community N score changed by 0.17 (-0.61 to 0.96) of its spatial expectation. Limitations: modelled deposition, perturbed coordinates, genus-level groups, spatial confounding of climate, Ca and forest type, and a short, low-deposition resurvey with large pseudo-turnover (median Sorensen 0.64).
